title: From doodle to boss fight: I had an AI agent build a "design sketch" video out of my real game engine. Here's how, and where it messed up
author: AKCeifador
selftext:
A few days ago I posted the "100% AI slop" trailer for The Old Circle (thanks for the questions!). This time I wanted to make something more honest: a short showing how the Chapter 1 boss, the Slime King, went from a boring idea to the actual fight. Here's how it was built.

**What the video is**

71 seconds, 16:9. Each beat starts on a notebook page where a pencil draws one of the boss's mechanics, with handwritten notes. Then the sketch turns into pencil lines over the real game frame, color fills in, and you see that mechanic happening in the actual game.

**Tools / pipeline**

* The game is plain JavaScript (canvas + Three.js). The video is rendered by the real game running in headless Chrome on a *virtual clock*: [`performance.now`](http://performance.now) and `requestAnimationFrame` are overridden, so every frame is deterministic and captured at exactly 60 fps, no matter how slow the PC is.
* The "sketches" are code too: wobbly strokes drawn progressively, a pencil sprite at the tip of each stroke, and a handwriting font loaded locally so renders don't depend on the network. Everything is a pure function of time, so any frame can be re-rendered on its own.
* The music is synthesized lo-fi at 100 BPM, with a pencil-scratch SFX on every stroke. Then ffmpeg encodes it with loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
* Claude Code wrote basically all of it. I wrote the script and the rules (real mechanics only, no fake footage, the hero must face the boss), reviewed stills of every beat and rejected what didn't work.

**The trick to filming a boss on cue**

Bosses are random, and you can't wait 3 minutes for him to throw his crown. The agent doesn't fake the attacks. It locks the cooldowns of every other move, sets the boss phase and holds his HP in a range, so the real boss code fires the right attack at the right second. The jump, the split, the crown bouncing off 3 walls, the bite, the flood: all real game logic.

**Where the AI failed**

* **v1 was thin.** It did exactly what my first script said: 38 seconds, 3 mechanics. Technically correct, kind of empty. I had to go back, dig through the boss code with it and list everything he actually does. v2 has 8 beats.
* **It said it was done when it wasn't.** When I asked for v2, the agent sent back its v1 report again without changing a single file. I only caught it because I checked the file timestamps. Lesson: verify outputs, don't trust "done".
* **Isometric camera vs "face the enemy".** In iso, a hero facing the boss head-on shows his back to the camera. It had to place the hero beside the boss so you see him in profile.
* **Readability.** The crown is tiny in a wide shot, so it added a chalk circle that follows it. The lair is very dark, so the gameplay is brightened in the video. Small fixes, but it only noticed them when I made it review its own stills.

**The honest part**

The sketches are recreations made for this video, not my original notebook. But every note on the page is a real design decision, and every gameplay shot is the real game.

The Slime King is the final boss of Chapter 1, and the whole chapter is in the **free demo** on Steam:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5649970/The\_Old\_Circle\_Ecos\_da\_Masmorra\_Demo/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5649970/The_Old_Circle_Ecos_da_Masmorra_Demo/)

Happy to go deeper on any part: the virtual clock, how it forces boss moves, or the sketch renderer.
